# Recap of Day 1

::: {.callout-tip}
## Summary of Day 1

- A Shiny app is a **folder** with `ui.R` (what the user sees) and `server.R` (what R does)
- UI and server talk **only through IDs**: `inputId` → `input$id`, `outputId` → `output$id`
- Each `*Output()` in the UI has its `render*()` partner in the server
- `render*()` and `reactive()` re-run **automatically** when the inputs they read change
- `eventReactive(input$button, { ... })` re-runs **only** when the button is clicked
- `uiOutput()` + `renderUI()` create inputs that depend on the data
:::

Open your project `my-shiny-app`, run the app and check it works. If you did not finish yesterday, copy the files of [`apps/05-explore-step4`](https://github.com/ottaviae/stat-shiny/tree/main/apps/05-explore-step4) into the project.

To publish the app, the online server ([Connect Cloud](09-deploy.qmd)) takes it **from a GitHub repository**. Today we put the project `my-shiny-app` on GitHub.

# Repositories management

The GitHub repositories are the folders containing the R Project:

## Create new repository

![Create a new repository that does not exist -- Step 1](../img/createNew.png){fig-align="center"}

This initializes a new GitHub repository, where you can provide different information concerning its characteristics

![Create a new repository that does not exist -- Step 2](../img/repoDefinition.png){fig-align="center"}

## Add existing repository

![Add an existing repository that does exist](../img/addRepository.png){fig-align="center"}

This option opens a window where you can navigate to your repository (i.e., a folder on your computer). When you do that, GitHub realizes that the repository does not exist as a GitHub repo, warns you of this and asks you whether you want to create a GitHub repo in that directory -- needles to say, say yes and do that.

## Publish the repositories

Once a repository is added (either by adding an existing one or creating a new one), it can be published and made available online for other people:

![Publish button](../img/publish1.png){fig-align="center"}

If you want your repository to be found by other users, remove the flag from the "Keep this code private":

![Define the publication policies](../img/publish2.png){fig-align="center"}

### `commit + push`

Everything is ready for the commitment.

1. Select specific files and commit them. The commit message is mandatory! It is useful for your future self, just to remember the changes you made, when and possibly why.

![Select & Commit](../img/commit1.png){fig-align="center"}

2. The changes must be pushed to GitHub:

![Select & Commit](../img/commit2.png){fig-align="center"}

3. Check whether the changes are live on GitHub:

![Check Commit](../img/commit3.png){fig-align="center"}

### Licenses

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## MIT

Anyone can use, modify, distribute, and  commercialize the software, provided that the original copyright notice and license text are included
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## GNU

Anyone can use, modify, and distribute the software. Any derivative work or redistributed version must be released under the same GPL license and with source code available.
:::

Summarizing the differences between the types of licences:

| MIT                                 | GNU GPL                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Can be used in proprietary software | Derivative works must remain open source            |
| Minimal restrictions                | Requires source code disclosure upon redistribution |
| Maximizes flexibility and adoption  | Ensures openness is preserved                       |
